title.en: Viracocha: Creation from Lake Titicaca and the Journey to the Sea
title.zh: 維拉科查：自的的喀喀湖創世與赴海之旅

region.en: Lake Titicaca / Tiwanaku (symbolic pin), Bolivia-Peru border
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖／蒂亞瓦納科（玻利維亞-秘魯邊境；象徵性定位）

texts.period: Recorded 1572 (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica, commissioned by Viceroy Toledo); principal MS: Gottingen University MS (trans. Clements Markham, 1907, public domain)

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica chs. 6-11 (1572), in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, London 1907 (public domain)

summary.en: In darkness Viracocha rises from Lake Titicaca and creates sun, moon, and stars; after a flood destroys the stone giants he repopulates the land, animating stones into peoples at Tiwanaku, Cacha, and Urcos; he sends two companions to teach, walks the Andes naming tribes, and departs westward across the sea at Manta, walking on the water.
summary.zh: 黑暗之中，維拉科查自的的喀喀湖升起，造日月星辰；洪水滅石巨人後重造萬民，於蒂亞瓦納科、卡查與烏爾科斯點石成人；遣二徒傳教，遍行安第斯點名部落，終於曼塔踏海西去。

sensitivity.note: Key sources are colonial-era chronicles commissioned to justify conquest; living Quechua and Aymara communities hold the heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento ch. 7 (Markham 1907): Viracocha rose from Lake Titicaca and made the sun, moon, and stars, commanding the sun: 'Thou shalt rise, and go up gradually to where thou art... and by thy beams thou shalt comfort and light the world.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento ch. 7 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento chs. 9-11 (Markham 1907): He made the peoples from stones: at Tiwanaku he fashioned the 'stone nations'; at Cacha he called out the men and women ('come forth from the caves and mountains'); at Urcos he left one man kept in stone? he named each tribe its place — and going west he came to Manta, where he walked over the sea and was seen no more. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento chs. 9-11 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish (colonial chronicle rendering Quechua oral tradition)
texts.canonical_translation: Clements R. Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, Hakluyt Society, London 1907 (public domain)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: CREATION FROM THE LAKE. The world began in darkness: there was no sun, moon, or stars, only a people of stone giants. Viracocha (Pachayachachic, 'teacher of the world'; Tici Viracocha) rose from Lake Titicaca on the island of the Sun and made the celestial bodies: the sun he commanded to rise and climb to its height, 'and by thy beams thou shalt comfort and light the world'; the moon he made brighter at first, then dimmer (the moon's pallor is the aition). The stone giants of the first age, too large and insolent, are destroyed — Viracocha floods the world (the unu pachacuti), leaving two? (in Sarmiento: none but the deep caves) — and the age of giants is judged a failure.

MIDDLE: THE MAKING OF THE PEOPLES FROM STONES. Viracocha now repopulates: at Tiwanaku he models the nations out of stone — men, women, and children, each tribe with its own dress and language ('to each he gave its tongue and its raiment') — and at Cacha (where he was stoned by the first? in some tellings he burned the fields in anger) he animates the sculpted stones, calling them out of the mountains, caves, springs, and rivers: 'Come forth, and remember him who created you.' The stones of Tiwanaku still stand as the unfinished 'stone nations' — the aition of the ruins. At Urcos he leaves a stone man as? (in Sarmiento: he left one kept 'in the shape of a man' as the idol which Yupanqui later carries to war); he sends two companions (his 'brothers' in some tellings, dressed as apostles — the Christian frame of the colonial scribe) along the coasts to teach, while he himself walks the inland road, naming the tribes and ordaining their settlements.

END: THE JOURNEY TO THE SEA. Viracocha travels the Andes 'as a king? as a pilgrim', calling each nation by name and sending them their lands; he teaches sowing, irrigation, and crafts. At Manta (Ecuador), with his two companions, he walks over the sea and is seen no more — 'and they say that he went over the water as if without it' — the departing god of the western sea, expected to return. The Inca state builds on this: the temple of Viracocha at Cacha (Raqchi) with its great central wall; the imperial theology in which the Inca is Viracocha's regent; and the 16th-century accident by which 'Viracocha' became the term the Andeans used for the Spanish strangers themselves — the returning god expected, and the conqueror received.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Andean cosmology (the lake as creation-point, Tiwanaku as the workshop of peoples), the political theology of Inca kingship (regency under Viracocha), the pilgrimage geography of Raqchi and Titicaca, and the colonial-era debate over the 'white bearded god' myth; it is the Inca corpus's most textually stratified narrative (Sarmiento's Toledo-commissioned version vs. Garcilaso's Christianized telling vs. the Tiwanaku archaeology).
narrative.zh: 太初黑暗無日月星辰，有石巨人族。維拉科查（『世界之師』）自的的喀喀湖日島升起，造日月星辰，命日：『爾當升起，漸登高處，以光耀普照安慰世界』；先使月明，後令月淡（月色之緣起）。首紀石巨人傲慢，維拉科查以洪水滅之。遂於蒂亞瓦納科以石塑諸族——男女童各具服飾語言——於卡查呼石人出洞出泉：『出來吧，記念造爾者』；蒂亞瓦納科石像即未成之『石族』，為遺址之緣起。於烏爾科斯留一石化人為像；遣二徒沿海傳教，己行內陸之路，逐一點名部落、定其居所，教播種灌溉技藝。終至厄瓜多爾曼塔，與二徒踏海而去，『行於水上如無水』——西方之海所逝之神，世傳其將復返。印加王權即其攝政；卡查神廟（拉奇）中牆猶存；殖民時代『白鬚神』之說使『維拉科查』成為對西班牙人之稱呼。功能：湖為創世點、蒂亞瓦納科為萬民工坊、印加王權神學、拉奇與湖之朝聖地理。

functions: Andean cosmology: Lake Titicaca as creation-point, Tiwanaku as the workshop of peoples
Political theology: the Inca as Viracocha's regent on earth
Pilgrimage geography: Raqchi temple and the island of the Sun
Colonial reception: 'Viracocha' as the Andean name for the Spanish

variants.name: Sarmiento de Gamboa (1572)
variants.summary: The Toledo-commissioned telling: flood, stone-giants, stone-nations, the walking journey, departure at Manta; politically framed to legitimize conquest (bias flagged).

variants.name: Garcilaso de la Vega (1609)
variants.text_tradition: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Part 1
variants.summary: The mestizo chronicler's Christianized version: Viracocha as a benevolent apostolic teacher, gentler and more evangelical — evidence of colonial reinterpretation in the diaspora genre.

variants.name: Tiwanaku archaeology
variants.text_tradition: Tiwanaku monuments (Bolivia); Viracocha portico (Gateway of the Sun)
variants.summary: The Gateway of the Sun's central staff-god figure (c. 500-1000 CE) is read by many scholars as the pre-Inca Viracocha image — the myth's material stratum predating Inca retellings by centuries.

primary_sources.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica
primary_sources.citation: 1572, chs. 6-11; principal MS: Gottingen University Library MS (Lat. Fol. 79). Trans. Clements R. Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, Hakluyt Society, London 1907 (public domain).

secondary_sources.work: John H. Rowe, 'Inca Culture at the Time of the Spanish Conquest'
secondary_sources.citation: Rowe 1946, in Handbook of South American Indians vol. 2 (BAE Bulletin 143) — the standard source-critical survey.
Urton 1999, Austin: University of Texas Press — the mythic corpus with Quechua sources.

source_urls.description: Project Gutenberg — Markham, Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (1907, public domain; Sarmiento's Historia Indica)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Sarmiento was commissioned by Viceroy Toledo to justify conquest; his history is politically framed. Prefer community and Quechua/Aymara scholarship in commentary; the Tiwanaku monuments are Bolivian national heritage.

title.en: Omama and the White People: Yanomami Creation as Told by Davi Kopenawa
title.zh: 奧瑪瑪與白人：雅諾馬米創世敘事（達維·科佩納瓦口述）

region.en: Yanomami territory, Roraima-Apaz?, Brazil-Venezuela border (symbolic pin at Demini)
region.zh: 巴西-委內瑞拉邊境雅諾馬米領地（象徵性定位於德米尼）

texts.period: Recorded 1980s-2000s by Bruce Albert with Davi Kopenawa; published 2010 (French) / 2013 (English): The Falling Sky, Harvard University Press

source.work: Davi Kopenawa and Bruce Albert, The Falling Sky: Words of a Yanomami Shaman (Cambridge MA, 2013) — Omama creation narratives

texts.license: Community-authorized publication (Kopenawa's own words); quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Omama, the first shaman, created the forest and its peoples; he caught the xapiri spirits from the heights and taught the shamans to call them; he wept for the future and his tears became the white people, who were foretold to destroy the forest; when the gold-miners' smoke rises, the sky itself will fall — the authorized Yanomami telling of creation and apocalypse.
summary.zh: 首薩滿奧瑪瑪造森林與眾生；自高處捕沙皮里神靈，教薩滿召之；為未來而哭，其淚化為白人，預言將毀森林；金礦煙起之時，天必將塌落——此為雅諾馬米人自授權之創世與末世敘事。

sensitivity.note: This record uses the community-authorized publication of Davi Kopenawa (Yanomami shaman) with Bruce Albert; shamanic song texts are quoted only as summary. Other Yanomami recordings without consent are not used.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky, ch. 3 (Omama): Omama, the first shaman, grew tired of the old world's silence; he made the forest and the rivers, caught the xapiri spirits in his? and released them into the mountains, and taught the first shamans to call them with songs — 'the xapiri dance in the mirror of the spirits.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky, ch. 3 (Omama); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky (the white people and the falling sky): Omama wept for what the forest would suffer; his tears fell and became the white people, and he foretold they would come to consume the forest's land; when the miners' smoke rises to the sky, the xawara epidemic smoke will grow so hot that the sky, exhausted, will fall and crush the earth. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of The Falling Sky (the white people and the falling sky); not verbatim.

texts.language: Yanomae/Yanomami (Nadahup? Yanomaman family), told in Portuguese with Bruce Albert
texts.canonical_translation: Davi Kopenawa & Bruce Albert, The Falling Sky (Harvard UP, 2013; trans. Nicholas Elliott and Alison Dundy)

narrative.en:
The Yanomami (Yanomae/Yanomami) of the Brazil-Venezuela borderlands have a creation corpus transmitted by shamans; the fullest authorized published telling is by Davi Kopenawa, the Yanomami shaman and spokesman, in The Falling Sky (2010/2013), dictated to the anthropologist Bruce Albert over decades of collaboration.

BEGINNING: OMAMA MAKES THE WORLD. Omama, the first shaman, the son of Yarorimi? (Kopenawa's account), found the primordial world silent and inhospitable; he made the forest and its rivers, set the animals and plants in their places, and raised the first shabono houses and the first humans. He then journeyed to the heights of the sky where the xapiri (the spirit-beings, the 'mirror images' of forest beings and ancestors) live in great houses; he caught the xapiri, brought them down, and taught the first shamans to call them with songs and yakoana snuff: 'the xapiri dance in the mirror of the spirits' — the shamanic vocation is thus Omama's apprenticeship gift, not a human invention.

MIDDLE: THE TEARS THAT BECAME THE WHITE PEOPLE. Omama, seeing what would come, wept for the forest; his tears fell to the ground and became the white people (napë) — and he foretold that they would come from across the sea to consume the land of the forest, hunting its ore and oil, building roads and mining gold: 'the napë did not fall from the sky; they are the children of Omama's tears.' Kopenawa's telling integrates this foretelling with the historical memory of contact (the road-builders of the 1970s-80s, the epidemics — xawara, the epidemic smoke — that killed Yanomami by the thousands, and the garimpeiro gold-miners of the 1980s).

END: THE FALLING SKY. The shamans know the world's fate: when the smoke of the miners' fires (and the oil-burning of the cities) rises too thick, the xawara epidemic-smoke will heat the sky's flesh; the sky, which is alive and exhausted, will grow dry and crack — 'and the sky will fall, and it will crush the earth and its forest'. The shamans' work — dancing the xapiri, cooling the sky, holding the forest's spirits — is the only thing that keeps the sky from falling now: the creation narrative is thus a charter of ecological duty and of Yanomami political speech ('the forest is alive... the sky is watching'). Kopenawa's book, awarded worldwide, made this telling the best-known Amazonian creation narrative in contemporary circulation.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Yanomami shamanic practice (the xapiri dances; yakoana), the ethics of forest-keeping, and the community's political discourse (land demarcation, mining bans); its authorized publication is itself a land-rights intervention, cited before the Brazilian Congress and UN bodies.
narrative.zh: 雅諾馬米創世之最完備之已授權出版文本為薩滿達維·科佩納瓦與人類學家布魯斯·阿爾貝數十年合作之《天空將墜》（2010/2013）。首薩滿奧瑪瑪嫌太初世界死寂，造森林江河，安萬獸萬木，立首座舍博諾長屋與初民；再赴天頂沙皮里神靈之大屋，捕沙皮里而釋於群山，教首批薩滿以歌與亞科阿那鼻煙召之：『沙皮里在神靈之鏡中起舞』——薩滿之職乃奧瑪瑪之傳授，非人自創。奧瑪瑪預見未來，為森林而哭；其淚落地化為白人（napë），並預言彼等將渡海而來，獵地礦油、築路掘金：『白人非天降，乃奧瑪瑪之淚所化。』科佩納瓦以此預言融匯接觸史：1970-80 年代之公路與疫病（xawara 疫煙）滅族之災、1980 年代金礦侵入。末世：礦火與城市油煙過厚，疫煙烤熱天之軀體；天乃活物，疲竭將裂——『天將墜，壓大地與森林』。薩滿舞沙皮里、冷卻天空、守林中之靈，為今日唯一不使天墜之功——創世敘事遂成生態職責與雅諾馬米政治言說之憲章。

functions: Charter of Yanomami shamanism: xapiri dances and yakoana as Omama's gift
Ecological duty: forest-keeping as the work that holds up the sky
Political speech: the narrative cited in land-demarcation and mining debates
Contact history integrated: tears-as-whites as the myth of colonial encounter

variants.name: Kopenawa's authorized telling (The Falling Sky)
variants.text_tradition: Dictated 1980s-2000s to Bruce Albert; Harvard UP 2013
variants.summary: The fullest published creation-apocalypse, told by a named Yanomami shaman with explicit collaboration — the community-authorized record.

variants.name: Bruce Albert's ethnographic apparatus
variants.text_tradition: Albert's fieldwork (1975-present) among the Yanomae of the Demini region
variants.summary: The book's notes and appendices supply the parallel mythic corpus (Omama's songs, the Yarorimi? cycle) with linguistic glosses — the scholarly frame around the authorized telling.

variants.name: Earlier ethnographic recordings (caution)
variants.text_tradition: Napoleon Chagnon's fieldwork corpus (1960s-90s); Lizot's recordings
variants.summary: Contested and ethically criticized collections; Kopenawa and Yanomami associations (Hutukara) have critiqued unconsented use — this record flags them and prefers the authorized text.

primary_sources.work: Davi Kopenawa and Bruce Albert, The Falling Sky: Words of a Yanomami Shaman
primary_sources.citation: Harvard University Press, Cambridge MA 2013 (trans. N. Elliott and A. Dundy); original: La chute du ciel, Paris 2010. Omama narratives: chs. 2-6.

secondary_sources.work: Bruce Albert, appendices and notes in The Falling Sky
secondary_sources.citation: Albert 2013, Harvard UP — ethnographic and linguistic apparatus documenting the Omama corpus and its parallels.
Community-authored materials on mining and forest defense (2010s) — the living political use of the narrative.
secondary_sources.note: Cited as community source per ethics protocol.

source_urls.description: Harvard University Press — The Falling Sky (Kopenawa & Albert, 2013)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: This record relies on the community-authorized publication (Kopenawa's own book with named collaborator Bruce Albert). Unconsented Yanomami recordings (Chagnon corpus) are flagged and not used. Shamanic song texts are summarized, not reproduced; land demarcation and mining remain active political issues — handle with care.
